facts.text: On this date in 1978, Muhammad Ali defeated Leon Spinks to reclaim the heavyweight title — becoming the first boxer ever to win the world heavyweight championship three times.
On this date in 1821, Costa Rica, Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, and Nicaragua all declared independence simultaneously — a single document signed in Guatemala City liberated five nations at once.
Monaco has a higher density of millionaires per capita than any country on Earth: roughly one in three residents qualifies, yet the nation covers less than one square mile.
The Philippines is the only country in the world where divorce remains fully illegal for non-Muslim citizens — a legacy of Spanish colonial Catholic law that has survived every modern reform effort.
Tokyo's greater metropolitan area, home to 37 million people, produces an economic output comparable to the entire GDP of Canada — one city roughly matching a G7 nation.
On this date in 1908, William Durant founded General Motors — a company that would go bankrupt exactly 101 years later, in 2009, and still survive.
On September 15, 2008, Lehman Brothers filed the largest bankruptcy in US history: $613 billion in debt, gone overnight after 158 years in business.
The New York Stock Exchange was founded under a buttonwood tree in 1792. The original agreement had 24 signatories and fit on a single page.
Saudi Aramco briefly became the first company worth $2 trillion in 2020. Its annual profit that year was larger than Apple, Google, and ExxonMobil combined.
The US penny costs 3.07 cents to manufacture. The government loses money on every one it mints, and has for over two decades.
On this date in 1977, Voyager 1 launched. It is now so far from Earth that a radio signal traveling at light speed takes over 23 hours to reach it.
On September 15, 1835, Darwin anchored at the Galápagos. He initially thought the finches were unrelated species — the insight that unified them came years later, back in London.
Your skeleton is not static. Almost every atom in your bones is replaced within a decade, meaning the skeleton you were buried with at 30 is largely not the one you were born with.
A neutron star packs more mass than the Sun into a sphere the size of a city. A single teaspoon of its material would weigh roughly a billion tons on Earth.
Trees in a forest share carbon and distress signals through underground fungal networks. A single Douglas fir can be connected to hundreds of neighboring trees simultaneously.
On this day in 1916, tanks entered combat for the first time at the Somme. The British called them 'tanks' as a decoy codename during shipping — and it stuck forever.
Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the construction of the Great Pyramid. The pyramid is that old.
On this day in 1935, Nazi Germany passed the Nuremberg Laws, stripping Jews of citizenship — just two years after Hitler was named Time's Man of the Year.
Oxford University was teaching students before the Aztec Empire existed. When Montezuma was born, Oxford had already been lecturing for 300 years.
The fax machine was invented before the telephone. Alexander Bain patented a working fax prototype in 1843; Bell's telephone came in 1876.

Saudade (Portuguese): a melancholic longing for something beloved and lost. Linguists consider it untranslatable — the word describes an emotion other languages can only approximate with entire sentences.
Vellichor (n.): the strange wistfulness of used bookshops, coined by John Koenig in 2012. It spread so fast that dictionaries now cite it as evidence that individuals can still mint genuine words.

On this date in 1835, Darwin's ship HMS Beagle arrived at the Galápagos. The Spanish sailors who named the islands chose 'galápago' — an old word for a riding saddle — because the giant tortoises' shells curved exactly like one.

Hiraeth (Welsh): homesickness for a home you cannot return to, or never had. The word carries grief, longing, and incompleteness simultaneously — a feeling most people recognise instantly despite having no word for it.

Sonder (n.): the realization that every passerby has a life as vivid as your own. Like vellichor, John Koenig invented it — yet it spread into common use so swiftly that the invented etymology is now widely mistaken for ancient Greek.
On this date in 2017, China's central bank declared ICOs illegal and ordered all proceeds returned — triggering a 40% bitcoin crash within days, yet BTC ended that year up over 1,300%.
On this date in 2022, Ethereum completed The Merge, switching from proof-of-work to proof-of-stake and cutting its energy consumption by roughly 99.95% in a single block.
Bitcoin's smallest unit, the satoshi, wasn't named by Satoshi Nakamoto — the community coined the term in 2010, and it took years before it appeared in any official documentation.
The DAO hack of 2016 didn't steal ETH — it drained 3.6M ETH into a child contract that had a mandatory 28-day delay, giving Ethereum developers the window to execute a controversial hard fork.
Blockchains don't store images or video — NFTs typically hold only a URL pointing off-chain, meaning the asset can vanish if the hosting server goes down, regardless of what the ledger says.

On this date in 2009, ImageNet launched publicly — the 14-million-image dataset that would quietly sit dormant until 2012, when AlexNet used it to cut image classification error by 41%, igniting the modern deep learning era.

On this date in 2017, Google Brain published 'Attention Is All You Need,' retiring recurrence from sequence modeling. Every major language model today — GPT, Gemini, Claude — is a direct architectural descendant.
GPT-4's training run is estimated to have consumed roughly 50 gigawatt-hours of electricity — comparable to the annual consumption of 4,600 average US homes, for a single training pass.

Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) was not invented for chatbots. The technique was first applied to video games and robotic locomotion; its use in language alignment only became standard practice after 2022.

Transformers generalize so aggressively that a model trained exclusively on text can, without retraining, solve visual reasoning tasks when images are tokenized — a capability researchers did not predict before observing it.
